title: The Two-State Vector Formalism of Qauntum Mechanics: an Updated Review
version: arXiv:quant-ph/0105101v2 (2007-06-10; v1 2001-05-21); also in Time in Quantum Mechanics, Lect. Notes Phys. 72, pp. 369-412, DOI 10.1007/3-540-45846-8_13. TeX source inspected: vaidman2.tex.
locators: Sec. I.B 'The two-state vector'; Sec. II.B 'The Aharonov-Bergmann-Lebowitz rule' (ABL formula, eq. labeled (ABL)); Sec. II.C three-boxes example; Sec. III 'Weak Measurements'; Sec. V 'Time Symmetry' incl. V.A 'Forward and Backward Evolving Quantum States', V.C 'The time-asymmetry', V.D 'If measurements are time-asymmetric, how the outcomes of measurements are time-symmetric?'
assumptions: Standard quantum theory assumed; TSVF presented as a time-symmetrized description using both a forward-evolving state |Psi> (from pre-selection) and a backward-evolving state <Phi| (from post-selection). Boundary conditions at both ends are stipulated descriptions of ensembles, not new dynamics.
conclusion: Authors' claims: TSVF is a reformulation of standard QM for pre- and post-selected ensembles, not a rival theory; the ABL formula gives intermediate-measurement probabilities conditioned on both ends; weak measurements reveal 'weak values' (eq. (wv) area of Sec. III); the symmetry between forward and backward evolving states is incomplete in practice because preparation can be corrected unitarily while post-selection cannot, due to the fixed memory arrow of time; the probability formulae are time-symmetric even though the concept of measurement is not.
proof_status: Authors' derivations read at the stated locators from the TeX source; not independently re-derived. The ABL rule's validity conditions are themselves contested in the literature (Vaidman's own PRA 57, 2251 (1998) 'Validity of the Aharonov-Bergmann-Lebowitz rule' found via CrossRef, not read).
dependencies: Pre- and post-selection, ideal (von Neumann) measurements, weak measurement interaction limit. Related formalism: time-abl-1964 (origin), time-aav-1988 (weak values).
open_questions: Does the two-time description carry any ontological commitment about the future existing, or is it an ensemble-selection device? The review distinguishes formalism from interpretation but the 'two-time interpretation' ontological reading is developed elsewhere (not obtained).
relevance: Primary anchor for the two-state formalism: gives exact ABL formula, weak-value construction, and an explicit statement of which time asymmetries remain (memory/creation asymmetry) inside a formally time-symmetric framework.
limits: Full text read from arXiv v2 TeX; the Springer LNPs pagination and section numbering may differ from the arXiv version. No independent numerical check. Title's 'Qauntum' typo is as-published on arXiv.

title: Bell's Theorem and Locally-Mediated Reformulations of Quantum Mechanics
version: Rev. Mod. Phys. 92, 021002 (2020); arXiv:1906.04313v2 (2020-02-17; v1 2019-06-10); DOI 10.1103/RevModPhys.92.021002. TeX source inspected: BellPaperRevision.tex; bibliography file RMPBibTexFile.bib used for exact locators of cited classics.
locators: Sec. I (future-input dependence; all-at-once framing); Sec. II (Bell's theorem; NFID assumption; lambda-independence Eq. (SI)); Sec. III (categorization of Bell-compatible reformulations); Sec. IV (Type IIA locally-mediated toy models); Sec. VI.B 'Type IIB models' (classifies TSVF and Transactional Interpretation); Sec. VI.C 'Models outside the framework' (superdeterminism; Many-Worlds treatment); Sec. VI.D 'Misconceptions' (determinism is not a presupposition; Bell 1981 quote); Sec. VII 'Conclusions'.
assumptions: Framework: models defined by probabilities over inputs (measurement settings a,b as free variables) and non-input parameters Q; Local Causality decomposed into (i) no future-input dependence (NFID), (ii) lambda-independence, (iii) continuous action (CA). Models must be in 'agreement' with QM to count as reformulations.
conclusion: Authors' claims: any QM-agreeing model must violate Local Causality, but a locally-mediated (CA-satisfying) class survives if NFID is relaxed: intermediate parameters on worldlines may depend on future settings, with all-at-once (boundary-value) solution rather than past-to-future unfolding; no retro-signaling is possible in these models; TSVF and Transactional Interpretation are Type IIB (future-input dependent but not spacetime-localized); superdeterminism violates lambda-independence instead and, in explicit QM-agreeing toy models (Brans 1988; Hall 2016), ends up treating settings as free inputs again, re-entering the framework; Many-Worlds 'outside the framework' recovers a Type IB effective model at the effective-Born-rule level (citing Maudlin 2010); determinism is not a presupposition of Bell's theorem (Bell 1981: 'It is remarkably difficult to get this point across, that determinism is not a presupposition of the analysis').
proof_status: Review; authors' framework definitions and toy-model claims read from full TeX. The Bell-theorem derivation itself was read but not re-derived here; its correctness is established literature (consistent with Griffiths 1984/Cramer 1986 bibliographies linking ABL/Bell lines).
dependencies: Bell 1964; Bell 1976/1977; causal-model framework (Pearl 2009); cited toy models (Costa de Beauregard 1953ff; Sutherland 1983/2017; Pegg; Price 1984/1997; Aharonov-Vaidman 1991; Cramer 1980/2016; Brans 1988; Hall 2016; Shimony-Horne-Clauser 1976; 't Hooft 2016).
open_questions: The authors state that generalizing Type IIA locally-mediated models to all quantum phenomena is an open 'grand challenge' (their wording); no general all-at-once reformulation of QFT exists on their account. Whether all-at-once boundary conditions imply any temporal-ontology claim is not addressed by the paper (our question, not theirs).
relevance: Primary anchor for retrocausal and all-at-once formulations: supplies the taxonomy (Type I/IIA/IIB), the exact assumption whose relaxation yields retrocausation (NFID), and the separation from superdeterminism.
limits: Full text read from arXiv v2 TeX; RMP pagination not mapped to section numbers (cited by section titles). Toy models in Sec. IV read at the level of construction and claims, not re-derived.

title: Everettian Quantum Mechanics
version: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy; first published 1998-06-03, substantive revision 2023-06-20 (page copyright 2023). Full text fetched and archived locally this date.
locators: Sec. 2 (measurement problem; rules 4a/4b); Sec. 3 (Everett's deduction; fundamental relativity of states, quoting 1956, 103 and 1957, 180); Sec. 3.2 (typicality measure m from constraints; Everett 1956, 123-8, 1957, 188-93); Sec. 5.2 ('no observer would ever be aware of any branching', quoting Everett's reply to DeWitt, Barrett-Byrne 2012, 254); Sec. 5.3 (all elements of a superposition real due to possible interference, quoting 1956, 150); Sec. 5.4 and Sec. 6 (typicality is not probability; 'fails to be empirically adequate in any standard sense' without auxiliary assumptions); Sec. 7 (DeWitt's splitting worlds vs Everett's rejection; Wallace's emergent worlds; Deutsch-Wallace decision-theoretic probability; self-location uncertainty strategies).
assumptions: Secondary exposition; assumes von Neumann collapse formulation as baseline. Reports Everett's own typicality (not probability) reading of the norm-squared measure, and the auxiliary-assumption structure of many-worlds reconstructions.
conclusion: Encyclopedia's assessment (author's, in a peer-reviewed SEP entry): pure wave mechanics is empirically faithful (typical relative records show the quantum statistics) but not straightforwardly empirically adequate; forward-looking probabilities require further auxiliary assumptions (decision-theoretic or self-location strategies); Everett did not hold that the world literally splits; all elements of a superposition are equally real for Everett because interference between them is always possible in principle.
proof_status: Secondary source; mathematical results reported with citations (Hartle 1968; Farhi-Goldstone-Gutmann 1989; Barrett 1999) but not reproduced.
dependencies: Everett 1957 (''Relative State'' Formulation of QM, Rev. Mod. Phys. 29(3), 454-462, DOI 10.1103/RevModPhys.29.454; already recorded as phil-everett at discovery depth in knowledge/philosophy/sources.jsonl; not duplicated here); Barrett & Byrne 2012.
open_questions: Whether any self-location or decision-theoretic strategy yields standard forward-looking probabilities without auxiliary premises is reported as an open research area; the entry does not settle it.
relevance: Primary anchor for Everettian time: branching as emergent (Wallace) vs relative records (Everett), and the exact status of 'the future is fixed/branching' claims with locators.
limits: Full text read as fetched (sections 1-9). The entry is one author's synthesis; Everett-primary passages are quoted with page locators, but those page numbers were not checked against primary scans (phil-everett remains discovery-depth).

title: Time Symmetry and Asymmetry in Quantum Mechanics and Quantum Cosmology
version: In Physical Origins of Time Asymmetry, ed. J. Halliwell, J. Perez-Mercader, W. Zurek, Cambridge University Press (1994); arXiv:gr-qc/9304023v2 (2005-06-21; v1 1993-04-18), report no. UCSBTH01-31. TeX source inspected: timesym2.tex.
locators: Sec. II (arrow of time in Copenhagen QM of measured subsystems); Sec. III 'A Time-Neutral Formulation of Quantum Mechanics for Cosmology' (probabilities p(alpha_n..alpha_1) = N Tr[rho_f P^n ... rho_i P^1 ... P^n], Eq. (3.1); 'the quantum mechanics of closed systems based on (3.1) need not have a fundamental arrow of time'; 'Lost also, when rho_f is not proportional to I, is any notion of a unitarily evolving state at a moment of time'); Sec. IV 'Classical Two-Time Boundary Problems'; Sec. V.B 'Impossibility of a Universe with rho_f = rho_i' (only trivial dynamics exactly decoheres); abstract ('initial and final density matrices cannot both be pure; if they are there is no decoherence and no prediction'); Sec. VI discussion of T-symmetric boundary conditions.
assumptions: Generalized quantum mechanics of a closed system: sets of alternative histories with decoherence functional; two-boundary generalization of ABL (their Sec. III explicitly credits ABL 1964) with initial and final density matrices rho_i, rho_f (not necessarily normalized).
conclusion: Authors' claims: a time-neutral closed-system QM exists in which all arrows arise from differences between boundary conditions (e.g., special rho_i, indifferent rho_f proportional to identity, which 'seem to fit our data well'); strong time-symmetric boundary conditions (rho_f = rho_i, or both pure) are inconsistent with an interesting quasiclassical domain; detecting a non-indifferent final condition is an empirical question about whether any system today can 'see' the final condition.
proof_status: Framework statements and the Sec. V.B result read from full TeX; the trivial-dynamics decoherence result was not re-derived. Empirical-fit claims ('final condition of indifference... fit our data well') are the authors' assessments.
dependencies: ABL 1964; Griffiths 1984; Hartle 1991; GH 1990; decoherence functional formalism.
open_questions: Which final conditions are observationally allowed is left as an open empirical program; the connection (if any) from a non-indifferent rho_f to temporal-ontology claims is not discussed by the authors (our question).
relevance: Primary anchor connecting ABL two-boundary structure with consistent histories in a cosmological setting; the key source for 'what is fixed about the future' in the histories family.
limits: Full text read from arXiv v2 TeX; CUP pagination not available; equations cited by number in the arXiv version.

title: The Physics of 'Now'
version: Am. J. Phys. 73, 101-109 (2005); DOI 10.1119/1.1783900; arXiv:gr-qc/0403001v2 (2004-05-21). TeX source inspected: pnow12.tex.
locators: Abstract ('Past, present, and future are not properties of four-dimensional spacetime but notions describing how individual IGUSes process information'); Sec. II 'A Model IGUS'; Sec. proof_status: Conceptual/model paper; robot model read; no formal theorems claimed.

relevance: Primary anchor for the Everett/histories-family treatment of objective passage vs block description: gives a locatable claim that passage is not fundamental while experience of passage is explained.

title: The Consistent Histories Approach to Quantum Mechanics
version: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy; first published 2014-08-07, substantive revision 2024-06-19 (page copyright 2024). Full text fetched and archived locally this date.
locators: Sec. 1 (CH as 'Copenhagen done right'; no measurement problem); Sec. 2.4 (single framework rule; principles R1-R4; unicity vs 'pluricity'); Sec. 4.2 (history projectors; chain operators; consistency conditions Eq. (16); generalized Born rule Eq. (17); 'the histories approach is time symmetrical in the sense that the rules for assigning probabilities do not single out a particular direction of time'); Sec. 5 (quasiclassical frameworks); Sec. 9.3 'Criticisms of and Objections to Consistent Histories' (Kent 1997; Bassi & Ghirardi 1999 PLA 257, 247 and 2000 JSP 98, 457; Griffiths & Hartle 1998 replies; Dowker & Kent 1996 set-selection objection; unicity abandoned as 'the principal stumbling block').
assumptions: Standard Hilbert-space QM; all time dependence stochastic; Born rule fundamental; single framework rule as a syntactic constraint on quantum reasoning.
conclusion: Entry author's claims: CH is a consistent completion of standard QM with no measurement problem and no conflict with relativity; its philosophical cost is denial of unicity (no single universally-true state of affairs at each instant); criticisms (contrary inferences, set selection) are answered by the single framework rule, while the unicity objection is acknowledged as the main reason for resistance.
proof_status: Secondary exposition by the founder of the approach; theorems reported, not reproduced. Authorship creates an advocacy risk, counterweighted here by the primary critical records time-kent-1997, time-dowker-kent-1996, time-kent-reply-1998.
dependencies: Griffiths 1984; Omnes 1988ff; Gell-Mann & Hartle 1990; Griffiths 2002 Consistent Quantum Theory (ch. 16 consistency argument cited).
open_questions: Set selection / preferred framework remains the central unresolved objection in the entry's own account (repeated by Kent 1998 and Schlosshauer 2005, Wallace 2008, per Sec. 9.3).
relevance: Primary anchor for the consistent-histories account of time: stochastic (never branching-world) time dependence, explicit time-symmetry of the probability rules, and the unicity/pluricity issue that bears directly on fixed-future claims.
limits: Full text read as fetched (sections 1-5, 9.3 in detail). Authored by the approach's founder; treat characterizations of critics with care and check against the critics' own abstracts (recorded separately).

title: The Cellular Automaton Interpretation of Quantum Mechanics
version: Springer, 2016 (publisher per Wharton-Argaman 2020 bibliography); arXiv:1405.1548 (v1 2014-05-22; source dated 2015-12). TeX source inspected: CAinterpretation_Dec_2015.tex.
locators: Sec. 'Motivation for this work'; Sec. 'Interpreting quantum mechanics'; Sec. 'Concise description of the CA Interpretation': subsection 'Time reversible cellular automata' (locality and time-reversibility definitions, Eqs. labeled (Dlattice), (CAevollaw)), subsection 'The CAT and the CAI' (ontological basis; templates; 'The universe is in a single ontological state, never in a superposition'), subsection 'Counterfactual definiteness' (explicitly denied for non-ontological operators), Sec. 'Conclusions' ('Correlations do not require superluminal signals, let alone signals going backwards in time'; hidden-variable small print identified as the assumed absence of strong correlations in the initial state).
assumptions: Cellular Automaton Theory (CAT): the universal Schrödinger equation admits an ontological basis mapping dynamics to a classical, local, time-reversible automaton; CAI takes this for granted even if the basis cannot be identified; quantum states are epistemic 'templates' (superpositions of ontological states).
conclusion: Authors' claims: quantum mechanics (including interference) emerges from deterministic local automata; collapse is basis-change to beables, no violation of Schrödinger evolution; the measurement problem is dissolved; no-go theorems are evaded via strong initial-state correlations (this is his stated route around Bell); counterfactual definiteness is NOT assumed; Lorentz invariance and positivity of the Hamiltonian are acknowledged open difficulties.
proof_status: Book-length program; selected sections read in TeX. Toy constructions (cogwheel models) not reproduced. No general construction proving the Standard Model or even generic Hamiltonians arise is claimed by the author.
dependencies: Hidden-variables literature; Bell's theorem; PQ formalism (Part II).
open_questions: Whether a local automaton with an approximately Lorentz-invariant, positive Hamiltonian continuum limit exists is acknowledged by the author as unsolved; whether the CAI's beables fix a unique foliation/time is not addressed in the sections read.
relevance: Primary anchor for superdeterminism's strongest deterministic reading: exactly what is fixed (all ontological states at all times by local reversible law) and what the author does and does not claim.
limits: Selected sections only (a ~460-page book); Springer pagination not mapped; chapters in Part II read only at heading level.

title: Rethinking Superdeterminism
version: Frontiers in Physics 8, 139 (2020), DOI 10.3389/fphy.2020.00139 (related DOI verified from arXiv abs page HTML, 2026-10-19); arXiv:1912.06462 (v1 2019-12-13). TeX source inspected: sd17.tex.
locators: Sec. I Introduction ('superdeterministic theories are not interpretations of quantum mechanics. They are... theories more fundamental than quantum mechanics, from which quantum mechanics can be derived'); Sec. III 'What?' (definition: 'a Psi-epistemic, deterministic theory that violates Statistical Independence but is local in the sense of respecting Continuity of Action'; rho(lambda|a,b) != rho(lambda); 'Free Choice' terminology criticized); Sec. III.A 'Retrocausality and Future Input Dependence' (retrocausality and teleology called misleading for deterministic theories; Future Input Dependence as operational property); Sec. III.B 'Disambiguation' (authors distinguish superdeterminism from retrocausality; some authors, citing Wharton and Price, use different boundaries); Sec. IV 'Common Objections' (free will, conspiracy, cosmic Bell tests, tobacco-company analogy); Sec. VI 'Experimental Test' (model-independent argument: prepare near-identical states with small, cool detectors at small time increments; deviations from Born statistics expected as time-correlations, climate-vs-weather analogy).
assumptions: Realism, reductionism, determinism; Statistical Independence violable; locality as continuity of action; hidden variables are known degrees of freedom resolvable at experiment's energy scales (scale-separation premise stated in Sec. VI).
conclusion: Authors' claims: superdeterminism is a candidate theory more fundamental than QM rather than an interpretation; it need not be retrocausal or conspiratorial; the standard objections trade on classical-statistics intuitions; a broad class of superdeterministic theories predicts detectable time-correlations in specially prepared repeated measurements, i.e., testable deviations from QM (their proposal, not an established result).
proof_status: Position/program paper with an experimental-test proposal; no model computation reproduced. The claimed model-independence of the test is the authors' argument, not a verified theorem.
dependencies: Bell's theorem; CHSH; Handsteiner et al. cosmic Bell test (cited); Palmer's invariant-set program; Wharton's Future Input Dependence terminology; Hossenfelder 2011 proposal.
open_questions: Does any explicit superdeterministic model reproduce all of QM while satisfying the scale-separation premise? (They argue no complete model exists yet.) Would the proposed time-correlation test survive quantum-limited noise analysis? Open by their own account.
relevance: Primary anchor for the modern superdeterminism debate: precise definition (violation of Statistical Independence), explicit disambiguation from retrocausality, and the only articulated model-independent testability argument in this lane.
